title: Wardrobe and Aftermath
premise: Tamsin Vasquez has spent eleven years writing postcards to a burned-down address, maintaining the fiction that their family died in the fire rather than fled it. When a stranger at their mother's funeral calls them by 'Aurelia'—a name from a life Tamsin buried—they learn the fire was no accident and someone is finally asking questions. Returning to the river town of Halloway, Tamsin must confront the uncle who orchestrated the blaze, the identity they abandoned to survive, and the truth that their silence protected the guilty as much as themselves. In the end, Tamsin chooses testimony over invisibility, burning the last postcard not as an ending but as evidence, and reclaims their name at the cost of the safe, small life they built.
about_author: Dominic Blackwood is the pen name of a former court stenographer who spent two decades transcribing other people's confessions before writing his own. He lives near a river he does not swim in, and this is his third novel.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. At their mother's funeral in the city, Tamsin performs grief flawlessly, deflecting condolences with practiced smiles. We see their ritual: postcards mailed weekly to a dead address. Emotional beat: controlled loneliness, the cost of a life built on erasure.

chapters.title: Aurelia
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A gaunt stranger at the reception says, 'You're Aurelia Vasquez,' a name no one has spoken in eleven years. He leaves a card—Halloway County Records—and vanishes. Emotional beat: vertigo; the past reaching through the present.

chapters.title: Postcards to Ash
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, with flashback fragments. Tamsin burns the stranger's card, then can't sleep, rereading old postcards never answered. We learn the family 'died' in the Halloway house fire of 2013. Emotional beat: dread hardening into compulsion.

chapters.title: The Uncle Who Sends Money
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A monthly deposit arrives from 'Uncle Marek,' the only surviving relative who knows where Tamsin is. Tamsin realizes the money may be hush money—and that the stranger's questions threaten the arrangement keeping them invisible. Emotional beat: suspicion curdling toward fear.

chapters.title: Downriver
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin takes a bus to Halloway, telling no one, carrying a box of postcards like contraband. The town is half-renovated, half-ruined. Emotional beat: the uncanny familiarity of a place one swore off forever.

chapters.title: The House That Wasn't Rebuilt
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The lot where the family home burned is now a memorial garden planted by neighbors—who believe three people died there. Tamsin meets Dee Okafor, the records clerk whose letter summoned them. Emotional beat: guilt among the flowers.

chapters.title: What the Records Say
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. Dee, an archivist reopening cold cases, shows Tamsin the fire report: accelerant found, investigation closed abruptly. Dee believes Tamsin's father set the fire—or was made to. Emotional beat: the thrill and terror of documentation.

chapters.title: Marek
chapters.summary: Marek's POV. Now a respected property developer, Marek learns Tamsin is in town and begins quietly pulling strings—calls to the sheriff, offers to Dee's supervisor. Emotional beat: polished menace; corruption as routine.

chapters.title: The Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin tracks down Rosa, a former neighbor, who reveals the family name change was Marek's doing—he 'helped' the survivors disappear after the fire. Emotional beat: gratitude revealed as captivity.

chapters.title: What Father Knew
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, deep flashback. Eleven years earlier: the father discovered Marek's embezzlement from the family business and planned to go to authorities. Three days later, the fire. Emotional beat: the child's-eye horror of adult betrayal.

chapters.title: The Stranger Explains Himself
chapters.summary: The stranger's POV (Jonah Reyes, insurance investigator). Jonah lost his own family to a Marek-connected arson cover-up and has spent years building a file. He needs a living witness. Emotional beat: shared damage, uneasy alliance.

chapters.title: Small Town Hospitality
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Intimidation begins: Tamsin's motel room searched, a dead bird on the car hood, a friendly deputy suggesting they leave town. Emotional beat: the machinery of quiet coercion.

chapters.title: Dee's Risk
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. Dee copies sealed files against orders and loses her job for it, handing Tamsin a ledger linking Marek to shell companies that bought the burned properties cheap. Emotional beat: sacrifice as solidarity.

chapters.title: The Postcard Trap
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah realizes Marek has kept the postcard correspondence monitored for years—the mail to the burned address was intercepted, proof Marek always knew survivors lived. Emotional beat: revelation as weapon.

chapters.title: Dinner with Uncle Marek
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Marek invites Tamsin to dinner, all warmth and veiled threat: he doubled their allowance, he can end it, he reminds them what disappearance costs. Tamsin smiles the ending smile—for the first time, at him. Emotional beat: power shifting hands.

chapters.title: What Survival Cost
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Alone, Tamsin reckons with the years of silence: the mother's depression, the friendships never made, the self amputated to fit a hiding place. Emotional beat: grief for the life unlived.

chapters.title: The Fire Again
chapters.summary: Marek's POV. Cornered, Marek orders the archive annex—where Dee's copied originals sit—set alight, repeating his oldest solution. Emotional beat: escalation; history threatening to rhyme.

chapters.title: Smoke Over Halloway
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. The annex burns; Dee and Jonah salvage the ledger; Tamsin, arriving too late, sees flames and chooses to run toward them instead of away. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into resolve.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Before the county grand jury, Tamsin says their real name aloud and testifies about the fire, the money, the years of managed silence. Marek's lawyer dismantles everything except the postcards. Emotional beat: exposure as liberation.

chapters.title: The Ledger and the Man
chapters.summary: Jonah's and Dee's POVs. The ledger plus intercepted mail corroborate Tamsin; Marek is arrested at his marina, still adjusting his collar. Emotional beat: justice arriving unglamorously, but arriving.

chapters.title: Last Postcard
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin writes one final postcard to the burned address—not to the dead family, but to the person they pretended to be—and burns it in the memorial garden. Emotional beat: mourning completed, identity reclaimed.

chapters.title: Wardrobe and Aftermath
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, months later. Tamsin stays in Halloway, working part-time in Dee's rebuilt archive, legally restoring the name Aurelia Vasquez while keeping Tamsin too—both selves, worn openly like clothes. Emotional beat: quiet, earned peace; survival finally priced fairly.
